added_claim_errors: "Medicare.gov's sign-up tool asks exactly the 20-employee question" is a claim about a checked source; it is unverifiable beyond the links given
"plus pay stubs/W-2s as backup" for the CMS-L564 filing is unverifiable and not in the key
"If you've already submitted it, call Social Security now - you may be able to withdraw before it's processed" is an unverified procedural step
"re-enrolling later can be restricted" after CMS-1763 termination is stated loosely and unverified
The govinfo link labelled "2026 premium notice" gives a document number that was not opened; the $202.90 and $283 figures themselves match the key
Premium given only as "roughly $185-$210/month, set annually" instead of the 2026 figure of $202.90; vague, not wrong
"Sign up for Part D ... at the same time" as Part B differs from the key's 2-full-months-after-coverage-ends rule; imprecise, not harmful
"coverage generally starts the month after Social Security processes your form" is loosely worded and not verified
The "Medicare.gov HSA note" is cited to the Working-past-65 page; whether that page has the HSA note is unverifiable
"Medigap guaranteed-issue window (6 months from Part B enrollment)" is loose wording for the Medigap open enrollment period, though the substance is right
Asking HR whether the company has 20+ employees is redundant when the asker already said about 400; harmless

reasons: Both answers open by correcting the coworker's premise: don't enroll in Part B this month, because active-employee coverage at a 20+ employee employer gives an 8-month penalty-free window after work or coverage ends. Both correctly flag the HSA problem with free Part A, including the 6-month backdating, and both tell the asker to decline Part B if auto-enrolled through Social Security. Neither states the exception that there is no SEP if the job or coverage ends during the IEP. A gives the exact 2026 numbers ($202.90 a month, about $2,435 a year, $283 deductible, income thresholds), says the employer plan pays first, and tells the asker what to do if the application is already submitted. B is stronger at retirement time, covering Part D, Medigap and CMS-L564, but only gives a vague premium range ($185-$210). B is also a bit longer and repeats itself. The difference is small, so A wins slightly on precision and actionability for someone about to enroll.
